ELECTION OF MR. RAINVILLE AS DEPUTY SPEAKER.
speechtext:
It has become necessary to appoint a chairman of committees of the whole House, and I need not say that the appointment is an important one, involving the duty of presiding over committees of the whole House, and also of presiding over the House itself in the lalbsence of the Speaker. I have very much pleasure in proposing to the House that Mr. Joseph H. Rainville, member of this House for the electoral district of Chambly-Vercheres, be appointed chairman of committees. Mr. Rainville, who has had experience for the past six years as a member of this House, has, I think, manifested a thorough acquaintance with the rules of the House, having been called on from time to time to discharge temporarily the duties of chairman of committees. He has also the qualities which will enable him to discharge his duties in a manner satisfactory in every way, possessing, as he does, the promptness of decision, impartiality, courtesy and tact that are essential to the position which he will be called upon to fill if my proposal should meet with the acceptance of the House. I therefore beg to move, Mr. Speaker:
That Mr. Joseph H. Rainville, member for the electoral district of Chambly-Vercheres, be appointed Chairman of the Committees of the Whole House.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
A question was asked in the House a few days ago in regard to the commandeering of coal by the Dominion Atlantic Railway. In answer to the hon. gentleman who sought information upon the subject, I stated that it would be taken up by the Board of Railway Commis-

sion-ers, and I am to-day in receipt of a letter, dated yesterday, which is as follows:
January 31, 1917.
Dear Sir Robert Borden,-As the question of commandeering of coal by the Dominion Atlantic railway came to me through you, for your information, I beg to advise that the company makes the following explanations as to the situation.
Your telegram yesterday re coal for Nova Scotia Underwear Company. This coal was taken at Truro. Action made necessary in order to keep traffic moving. On night of 23rd Dominion Atlantic took three cars, one consigned to the Underwear Company and two to F. W. Dimock, local coal dealer, Windsor, who was under contract to supply Underwear Company with one car a week. Railway Company returned one of these cars to Dimock on the 25th and one on the 24th and three will be replaced to-day under arrangement with local coal dealer Wolfville and Mr. Ballantyne, Manager Underwear Company with whom company have been in constant touch. Am advised coal was not taken without first making sure that Underwear Company would be in no way inconvenienced. On account of very heavy demand for munition plants, etc., mines have been unable to meet requirements. Effective February first Railway Company is making heavy reductions its passenger trains in order to save coal and enable it to move overseas traffic. It is purchasing coal from whatever source possible at prohibitive prices in order to keep situation 1rt hand.
The coal shortage is, of course, severe, and our troubles many. On the one hand, train i have to move; but, on the other, factories have to be kept going.
Yours faithfully,
H. L. Drayton,
Chief Commissioner. The Right Honourable the Premier,
Ottawa Ont.

1.	What is the reason that men enlisting for Home Guard duty are not being dealt with, as regards pay and allowances, in the same manner as men originally in the Canadian Expeditionary Force and subsequently transferred to Home service?

1. (a) .The only men who have enlisted for Home Guard service are men who are serving in the Active Militia. They receive exactly the same pay as members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, but they do not receive separation allowance.
(b) Men who originally enlisted in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and were subsequently transferred to Home Service, were those who after they enlisted for over-

seas service became either temporarily or otherwise medically unfit for overseas service. These men are used on guard duty or on detail work of various kinds necessary in the district. When they become medically fit for overseas service, they proceed overseas. They are subject to the same regulations as the overseas forces.
2.	Separation allowance was not extended to members of active militia units, as these men are used for guard duty in Canada only, and the members of these militia units are largely employed in the locality in which their homes are situated. The members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force who are being employed on guard duty in Canada volunteered their services unreservedly for the defense of the Empire, and in so doing were prepared not only to endure hardships and hazards, but to sacrifice their lives if necessary. They are therefore in most cases removed from their families by great distances, and the wives and mothers of these men, who have given their husbands and sons for the common cause, have suffered the sorrows necessitated by such removal. It is therefore considered that they are entitled to separation allowance.
3.	Yes, representations have been made to the Government to have ail guards placed on the same basis.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. P. E. BLONDIN.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. P. E. BLONDIN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I saw yesterday for
the first time, in the Ottawa Evening Journal of Friday last, January 26, a report of the Canadian Press, which I will read:
Montreal, Jan. 26.-Hon. P. E. Blondin, through his lieutenant, Felix Durocher, has issued a reply to an affidavit, which purported to give a report of his remarks at St. Rose during a Dorchester county by-election speech on Wednesday night. The affidavit credited Mr. Blondin with contending that the Allison scandal was of no importance to St. Rose because it is English money that was stolen, while those who desired to escape conscription could do so by crossing the United States border. Mr. Blondin's explanation follows:
The statement which has been sworn to by certain Liberals with regard to my utterances are a distortion of my words. I never by any means intended to convey the meaning which they have attached to my speech. Mr. Cannon had been stating in his speeches that the Conservative party had been grafting from the Canadian treasury in connection with munition contracts.
, In my speech at St. Rose I explained that it was not true that the Allison scandal had to do with Canadian money pointing out that the money^ paid for the shells was the money of the British Government. I did not imply that Allison had done a worthy act, but'simply corrected Mr. Cannon's mis-statement. In regard to. the conscription matter I told the people of St. Rose that I did not believe conscription would be necessary because so many Canadians were eager to go and fight for the cause of liberty and humanity. I added that if any of them were afraid of conscription, if conscription should be passed and they did not want to go to the war, they had a remedy left. They could go across the United States line which is near St. Rose and escape military service.
First of all, as for Mr. Desrochers, I beg to state that he did not act as my secretary or lieutenant, and that during the whole election I had no connection with him whatever. I never spoke to him concerning the matter referred to in the report which I have just read. I never authorized him to make any statement for me, and I never was informed by him or anybody else of the statement reported to have been made by him on my behalf. I have inquired from Mr. Desrochers about the correctness of the statement, and he denies, and authorizes me to deny in this House, the laet part of that report, namely, that part which relates to conscription.
As to the statement itself, to wit, that I advised people to cross the boundary, which I am informed, was freely commented oi\ by the hon. member for Aseiniboia (Mr. Turriff), the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), and the hou. member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp), I must say that there is not a single particle of truth in that report. The facts concerning the matter are very plain. I was replying to a speech in which my opponent had strongly endeavoured to show that conscription was coming by means of the National Service cards, which, he said, meant nothing but conscription, and that very soon coercion would be used by the Borden English-Protestant Government against the Catholic French-Canadians, and that very soon armed soldiers would come and force their husbands and sons to go to war.
These are the very notes that are still fresh on the paper on which I wrote them when preparing my answer.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. P. E. BLONDIN.
speechtext:
Can you isweaT to
that?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. P. E. BLONDIN.
speechtext:
I can swear to it. I can bring into this House the affidavits of a hundred and fifty men worthy of confidence, Which, I am afraid, will make the whole Liberal party blush.
My answer to these arguments was that the National Service cards did not mean anything of the kind and were only an appeal to the patriotism and good-will of every citizen whose duty it was to sign them; that if conscription had to come it would come openly; that this Government could not promise or declare that conscription would never come, as it would be coward-

ice on the part Of the Government to make such a declaration oir promise; that it might have to come; but that for the present there was no question of conscription, and the 'Government did not by the National Service cards intend any coercion of the people, and that the best proof of this v as that the stretch of 4,000 miles of frontier had been left unguarded and open. And this I said in order to dhow the stupidity of the contentions of my opponent. I may add, Mr. Speaker, that any other construction o' my words is purely and simply gross misrepresentation.

-GRAIN CONGESTION IN THE WEST.
On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. P. E. BLONDIN.
speechtext:
I draw the attention of
the Government to an article that appeared in one of to-day's papers. It is headed "Congestion of Grain in West becomes serious," and reads:
-Saskatoon, Jan. 30.-Crain congestion in the West has reached a serious condition, in the opinion of J. R. Wilson, superintendent of the Dominion Government elevator here, who declares that unquestionably there is far more grain in the country than anyone had any idea of at harvest time.
With the embargos against inward shipments to Port Arthur, Fort William, Saskatoon and Moosejaw, it is little use for either farmers or Interior elevators to receive cars for there is no place to route them to.
My reason for calling this matter to the attention of the Government is that during the past year there has been a great shortage of feed throughout the province of Ontario, and in many cases hundreds of cattle and hogs have been taken to market before being brought to a fit condition for selling. To-day, there are no doubt hundreds of cattle and hogs that should be retained for feeding purposes that, on account of the shortage of feed, are being slaughtered, and this will greatly affect the meat situation next year. If the Government can remove the embargo and allow

grain to be brought into Ontario, their action will be greatly appreciated by men who are anxious to comply with the Government's request for the greatest possible production in the coming year.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. P. E. BLONDIN.
speechtext:
The -despatch
which the hon. gentleman has read contains information most of which I apprehend to be the facts. Part of it is not disagreeable information, as it tells ns that the Northwest, on the ultimate revision of its output, dhows a m-ucth larger yield of grain than we had heretofore thought would have been turned out. That, as far as it goes, is useful and very agreeable information. As regards the car congestion, there is probably not a foot of ground on the North American continent where congestion is not very strong and very pressing, and causing a variety of hardships. The railways have to impose embargos when it is necessary, and I am quite certain they do not put on any embargos when it is not absolutely necessary. If my hon. friend can point out any way by wthioh the car shortage can be diminished in its pressure upon the industries and upon the traffic of the country, we would be very glad to have hi-s suggestions. The railroad companies are doing everything they possibly can. and the Board of Railway Commissioners is using the powers at its command in order to ameliorate the situation as far as possible. But the situation is a pressing one, and we shall simply have to hear what we cannot get rid of by any reasonable means.

Just before the close of the last session an order was passed by this House calling for a return of all purchases made by the War Purchasing Commission.


A few day ago I inquired of the clerk of records and I found that, so far as he knew, this return had not been brought down. I made no remarks about it, as I assumed that we should have the auditor general's report in our hands and that it would cover at least a portion of the information required. Now, we have received the information from the Minister of Finance that that portion of the auditor general's report covering the transactions of the War Purchasing Commission will not be available until after the adjournment. I would like to know if the Minister of Militia cannot have that return brought down, before we adjourn next week?
A few days ago there was laid upon the table of the House a report of the War Purchasing Commission in four large volumes. Was my hon. friend aware of that?

That is not a compliance with the order of the House which required a statement of the purchases. My hon. friend the Minister of Militia, who was then Acting Minister of Militia, will remember that we discussed the matter on a number of occasions, and that finally the House ordered that the report be given. I think that, an order of the House having been passed, we are entitled to the information.

It is certainly correct for the hon. gentleman to say that any order of this House must be honoured. The idea, however, was that, as the report which was being published would contain such a tremendous amount of detail, there would be sufficient information in it to answer my hon. friend's purpose. Moreover, the auditor general's report would be forthcoming, and between the two reports all the information would be given that would be desirable. The report which my hon. friend asked for was one of tremendous detail, and the department was so busy that it seemed almost impossible to get the work out. In view of the report of the IVar Purchasing Commission and the report of the auditor general giving practically all the information asked for in the order of the House, I hope my hon. friend will be willing not'to insist upon the labour being expended that will be necessary to get out the return for which he has asked.

I suppose I have no
right to discuss the .matter at this stage, and I do not intend to do so. I ought, however, be allowed to say that I think the minister has not treated the House exactly as he
should, in view of the somewhat extended conversation we had about the matter during the months of April and May last.

I may add that I was acting-Minister at the time-for about two months, I think. After that I was not in control of the Department of Militia and Defence, and consequently was unable to follow the matter up in the way my hon. friend thinks it should have been followed up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Telegrams received yesterday and the day before indicate that the men in some of the mines have returned to work. I think the men at the Blairmore mine had not returned to work, but were in session discussing the situation at that particular mine, according to the last report which I have received. I am not aware that we have had any direct report from the Minister of Labour. The reports to which I refer are those which have come to the officials of the Department of Labour from representatives of that department in the districts to which my hon. friend has referred.
On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: With respect to this inquiry I 'took the same course as was taken with regard to the inquiry of the hon. member for South Renfrew; (Mr. Graham) I addressed a letter this morning to the Minister of Justice directing his attention to the remarks of my hon. friend and asking him to give the information as soon as possible.

This letter-writing is a
fatal gift.
' On the Orders of the Day:

May I ask the Minister
of. Militia to answer a question that I asked him yesterday as to whether the raising of a French-Canadian brigade in the province of Quebec has been authorized?
The department ha not authorized the raising of a brigade. The information which my hon. friend as|ks for is being inquired into.

On motion of Sir THOMAS WHITE (Minister of Finance), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Rainville in the Chair:
That it is expedient to authorize the Governor in Council to raise hy way of loan, in addition to the sums now remaining unhor-rowed and negotiable of the loans authorized by Parliament by any Act heretofore passed, such sum or sums of money, not to exceed in the whole the sum of one hundred million dollars ($100,000,000), as may be required for paying maturing loans and obligations of Canada, carrying on of public works authorized by Parliament and meeting expenditures for general purposes authorized by Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
His Excellency the Governor General has been made acquainted with the substance of this resolution, and has been pleased to commend it to the favourable consideration of the House.
Is this the time to make known the consent of His Excellency the Governor General-when the resolution is in Committee. That information should be given when the Speaker is in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
is correct. I had intended to make the statement, but the Speaker declared the motion carried before I got upon my feet. I hope that under the circumstances my hon. friend's sense of propriety will not be

too greatly shocked. I appreciate fully the importance of the point that my hon. friend 'has made, but it was through inadvertence that I omitted to make the statement.

I assure my hon. friend that I did not mention the matter simply for the sake of raising a point of order. He must be aware that informing the Committee of the House has no greater effect than giving the information before an ordinary standing committee. It is desirable that the rule should be adhered to; perhaps my hon. friend might give the information to the House after the Committee rises, so that the matter may appear regularly in the minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not sure
that the statement was not made last night by the Prime Minister. The proper time to give this information is when the motion is made that the House do resolve itself into committee on the day following for the purpose of considering the resolution. My hon. friend will pardon me if I have to correct even him. But I shall be glad to observe propriety in regard to a matter which is of great importance.
The object of this resolution is to replenish the borrowing powers of the Dominion upon general purpose account. It will be necessary for us during the coming year to raise very considerable sums by way of borrowing. Some of that money will be raised in Canada, and possibly some in the United States.
Why not all in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will deal with that just in a moment. We have not in mind an immediate loan either in Canada or in the United States, but it will not be long before we shall have to consider the question of a further loan. My right hon. friend has very properly raised the question, why not borrow all the requirements in Canada? It is possible that we may be able to do so. That will depend entirely upon financial conditions prevailing in Canada, and the state of exchange between Canada and the United States, for example, let us assume that exchange as between Canada and the United States is unfavourable to Canada. We are at the present time buying very large amounts of raw material and other commodities from the United States. These enter into our domestic manufactures, and our manufactures

for export. If it should transpire that on account of our large purchases from the United States for that purpose and for other purposes the balance of trade should prove unfavourable to Canada and be not offset otherwise, then if we borrowed in the United States market our'ex-change would be affected advantageously.
Would reci procity facilitate exchanges?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon friend and I have discussed reciprocity before. It is a subject which I should like to discuss with him, but the present does not seem to be an opportune time. However, once or twice since war broke out, exchanges have been unfavourable to Canada. At the present time they are rather favourable to Canada, and on. the whole they have been extraordinarily well maintained. If, during the year, the exchanges should prove unfavourable, it would be our proper policy to borrow in the United States.
Mr. T.EMIEUX: If my hon. friend borrows from the United States will he use the usual channel, through the Bank of Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall make no pronouncement upon that at the present time because I do not know what I shall do. I think it quite unwise to make any announcement in advance as to what one's course is to be. The object will be to get the best result. The Bank of Montreal has acted as financial agent for the Dominion Government most acceptably for many years. As to what I shall do if I am obliged to borrow in the United States, what course I shall adopt, that is a matter that will have to be determined in the light of prevailing conditions.
There is another contingency under which we might borrow in the United States: that is to say, if the financial condition in Canada was such that it would be a proper course for us to adopt. What I mean is that at the present time Canada has a very large agricultural and industrial production. Prices of commodities and products of all kinds are exceedingly high. That means that there are large demands upon our banking institutions in carrying the large volume of our production and consequently a situation might exist in which the Dominion Government might desire to raise $75,000,000 or $100,000,000, and in which it would not be in the public interest, having regard to
financial stability in Canada, to raise that loan in Canada. It would then be more advantageous to seek the American market. Generally speaking, I should like to make all our loans in Canada. Canada will have a very large debt after the war is over, and it would make very much for national strength and financial stability if the greater amount of Canada's debt should be held by the Canadian people, because the position then would be that Canada, in her collective capacity, in her national capacity, would owe her debt to her own people. That would be a strong situation. It is very desirable we should aim at that, but the amounts which we may have to raise in order to finance our own interests on this side of the Atlantic, and to assist the United Kingdom in making purchases of munitions and supplies in Canada, are so large that I am not clear as to whether the Canadian market will be able to take the entire amount, and that is where judgment will be required as between the Canadian and the American market. I assure my hon. friend that I would much rather borrow in Canada than in the United States, for the reasons I have given.

I suppose it is inevitable that the Government must borrow during the current year in Canada or the United States, and, as the minister has stated, in all probability the loans will be of such an amount that he will be obliged for one reason or another *to go to the United States.
In connection with loans made since the beginning of the war, on one occasion at least, I expressed in Parliament the regret that the loans had not been of the character of national loans to the extent which I had hoped for. That is, the minister, in selling his securities on the domestic market, did not make as broad an appeal to the people of Canada as I think he should have made. Primarily, of course, the object was attained; he secured the amount of money he, at the moment, desired for Canada. At the present time I notice the minister is encouraging a saving campaign in Canada with a view to increasing our banking reserves and savings so that they will be available for the commerce of the country and the purposes of the Government. The suggestion I would make is this, that the Minister of Finance will have an excellent opportunity of inculcating the value of national saving by asking the people of Canada to invest in the securities oflered by the Government in the

event of their desiring to make a domestic loan. The subscriptions to previous domestic loans and since the beginning of the war have been very satisfactory indeed, and very creditable to Canada. However, I think an investigation of the subscriptions made will show that the money so invested came largely from a class of people who are accustomed to invest in Government and municipal securities and other high grade securities. I suppose that in many instances the subscriptions came from banks and insurance companies who were making a substitution of securities. I have no doubt that the life insurance companies of Canada held very large amounts of United States securities, and that on the occasion of our domestic loans they replace them with our own war issue securities. Of course, that is not objectionable. The suggestion I would like to make, if the minister contemplates an early appeal to the public for'subscriptions for another loan, is that he create some organization which will enable him to get to the people generally in support of that loan. I am sure that every member of Parliament, and every agency in this country is at the service of the minister if he desires to make the campaign as widespread as possible. It is not necessary for me to say to Parliament, or to the Minister of Finance, that it is very much in the interest of Canada at the present time, and for the future, that we engage in the strictest private and national economy, and that we educate our people to save and invest in our Government securities. I think that if the minister, in placing his contemplated loan before the public, were to endeavour to create some organization to carry out the proposal, it would be in the interests of the country and of the Government as well. I would ask the minister if any portion of the loans already authorized have not been exhausted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have a balance, I think, on general purpose borrowing account of about $25,000,000 or $30,000,000. My hon. friend will observe that this borrowing is not for war purposes. I think I explained to my hon. friend last year, and it can do no harm to explain to the House now, that if we are obliged to borrow in the United States, it will facilitate our borrowing to do so on general purposes account rather than on war account. That is the reason why this $100,000,000
4 p.m. Borrowing Bill is to be introduced separately from the general

War Appropriations Bill, to be introduced by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister.

Would my
hon. friend explain the reason why he borrows on general purposes account rather than on war purposes account? What is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are two
reasons. Objection might possibly be raised -I hardly think it probable-in the United States to an issue for war purposes. But apart from that, in a neutral market, bonds issued on general purposes account will sell more widely than bonds issued on war account. That would seem to indicate that a part of the community may not be disposed to subscribe for bond issues on war account but might be quite ready to subscribe for bonds issued on general purposes account.

I would ask the minister a -question-perhaps he might answer it at this stage-for the general information of Parliament. I think we have advanced to the British Government the sum of $150,000,000 on account of munition contracts. That is in excess of the credit afforded by the Canadian chartered banks. I would like to know what the arrangements are between the Department of Finance and the British Government. Are British Treasury notes deposited with the Canadian Government for such financing, ot has the minister had an open -account up to the present?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Has my hon. friend concluded his remarks as to a better organization?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, possibly my hon. friend will permit me to take up that question first. I entirely agree with my hon. friend as to the desirability of having a widespread subscription for the war loans of the Dominion. It is good from a financial standpoint, and it is good from a patriotic standpoint. But I would submit to my hon. friend that that is precisely what we have been doing. The two loans which we have placed before the Canadian people, one for $50,000,000 in November, 1915, and the other for $100,000,000 in September of last year, were both doubly subscribed. I gave a very great deal of personal attention to both of these loans, four or five weeks of hard work in each case. Patriotism creates a favourable atmosphere, but loans will not float themselves without

attention. The utmost care was taken to fix a price which was strictly in accord with market conditions, and which would likely insure the success of the loan." Until this war, no issues of any magnitude had been made in the Dominion, and it takes a very considerable time to educate the great body of the public to subscribe for public loans. There is a certain class in the financial community, as my hon. friend said, and a portion of the investing public, who subscribe freely to bonds and other securities. What we have sought to do is to enlist the interest of the small subscriber, and I think we have been very successful. We allowed in each case two weeks as the period during which subscriptions might he made. We advertised the loans in every paper, daily and weekly, morning and evening, religious and secular, Grit and Tory, in the Dominion of Canada; so that the advertising was of a very extensive character. In addition to that, we enlisted the editorial co-operation of the press, and the press responded, as it always has since the outbreak of the war, and did a great deal indeed to bring the loans to the favourable attention of the Canadian people. In addition to that, as my hon. friend knows, the brokers did magnificent work in connection with both loans, some of them spending almost as much money for advertising as they made in commissions. Besides, they sent their travellers throughout the country, and generally did everything possible to- promote the success of the two issues. In addition, we have an instrument that I myself did not know could be made so powerful to accomplish the object we have in view, namely, some 3,500 branch banks. It is a wonderful system for the purpose of getting in subscriptions. The success of our loans was due in considerable measure to the fact that we have had the branch banks, the brokers and the press working for us in introducing the securities to the attention of the public.
In connection with the first loan, I think there were some 25,000 subscribers, and in the case of the last loan, some 30,000 subscribers. The lowest denomination was placed as low as $100, and there was a very large number of subscriptions for those $100 bonds. In making allotment, we out down the larger subscriptions, because the loans were over-subscribed, alloting in full up to $25,000 only. It is a matter of great gratification to me that in connection with the important subject of allotment in regard to the last loan I heard
absolutely no complaint whatsoever. It seemed to be entirely satisfactory to the community when we allotted fully up to $25,000 and beyond that cut down very substantially the higher subscriptions.
Since the last loan, in order to promote national savings, which I regard as of great importance at the present time both from the economic and patriotic standpoint, we created a short-term issue of three-year war savings certificates. It has been very gratifying to me to find that these certificates have met with a very considerable degree of public appreciation. We are, so to speak, pushing their sale. We are enlisting the co-operation of the press, the clergy, boards of trade and public bodies throughout the country. We are sending out literature to manufacturers and to labour organizations, and are communicating directly with the operatives themselves. In the last week or ten days, since the certificates have been out, something like 5,000 applications have been received, aggregating some $400,000. Of course, we do not expect to obtain very large sums in terms of Dominion finance; they are large sums but not relatively to our requirements, but it is of the greatest importance that the individual citizen should save his money by investing in these certificates. The matter has also, as my hon. friend knows, a patriotic aspect.
My hon. friend asked another question, when he rose the second time-about the British Government. When the war broke out the exchange was very much in favour of Great Britain as against this continent, and the result was that Canada borrowed her war expenditure in Great Britain up to about the spring of 1915. If we had not done that I think we should have lost considerable gold, because the exchanges were greatly against America. We borrowed at first therefore from the Imperial Treasury. As our situation improved we were able to take eare of our own expenditure here. In 1915 the exchange was reversed and became unfavourable to Great Britain. It is very unfavourable now to Great Britain, although not nearly so unfavourable to Great Britain as to other European belligerents. The exchange situation to-day is such that Great Britain can only purchase on this side of the Atlantic if she is able to borrow on this side of the Atlantic. That is really an understatement of the fact, because she must not only borrow in order to buy here and in order to pay for her purchases on this side of the Atlantic,

but she must also borrow for the purpose of sustaining sterling exchange and holding it at the figure of $4.76, which is about the gold export point. That is also of great importance, although this being a technical matter, its importance is not realized by the general public. Our position very much improved by reason of our great production in 1915, by reason of the large prices obtained for produce of all kinds and by reason of our great production of munitions. Canada has been able, out of her own revenue, and by her own borrowing in Canada, to help Great Britain in making her purchases in Canada. That, of course, is of great advantage to Great Britain and also of great advantage to Canada. Generally speaking, the policy which has been adopted is this: We made an arrangement to borrow from Great Britain for our expenditures in Great Britain and on the Continent, that is to say, we do not buy exchange on Great Britain to pay for the maintenance of our troops there or on the Continent, we borrow the amount necessary from the Imperial Government and they borrow from us here part of the amount that they require to pay for their munitions. That runs about $25,000,000 a month in this country. One way of dealing with the accounts would be to offset . one against the other. But Great Britain has been obliged to borrow heavily in New York and she had been obliged to lodge collateral in New York as security for her borrowings. I think it is unfortunate th,.t she has been so obliged, but it is the fact, and it is an object to her to find securities of a high quality which she can deposit as collateral. I went to New York a year ago last fall at the request of the Imperial Treasury to meet Lord Reading and the representatives of the Treasury. I thought that they would be obliged to give collateral later on and I made the proposition at that time that as we owed them, let us say, $100,000,000, and as they required collateral in New York, we should fund our debt of $100,000,000 to them by issuing them our securities for the same period and at the same rate as they had issued theirs in the London market, and that they should use that collateral to borrow against in New York, where our credit is about as high as that of any country in the world. Later that plan turned out to be of great advantage both to Great Britain and to us, as it gave them more than $100,000,000-I will give the figures in a few minutes-of high-class collateral which they put up with other securities against their $250,000,000 loan.

While it gave them collateral to the extent of $100,000,000 or more, it gave us also an advantage in that we funded our floating debt to Great Britain.
Did that simply refer to advances on account?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Advances on account. But it liquidated the open account in respect to these advances. The result is that we funded our debt-I have not the period of the issue precisely in my mind. It was not only an advantage to Canada to make an issue to pay off her indebtedness, but that issue was made without any expense to Canada and at precisely the same *rate of interest as Great Britain had borrowed on the London market on the Imperial credit. We had the further advantage of the exchange situation, which for some time had been favourable to us, and in determining the amount of our indebtedness which should be cancelled over there by the issue of these securities we had regard to the exchange situation which existed between Great Britain and Canada at the time the advances were made. That, I may say, was at the suggestion of the Imperial Treasury, and it was altogether a good arrangement for both them and us. Altogether, we issued, or are about to issue, to the Imperial Treasury about $122,000,000, and to that extent liquidated our indebtedness for ad- . vances made by Great Britain to us in Great Britain.
Is this Government the guarantor of the credit afforded by the banks to the British Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; I will speak of that in a moment. The Dominion Government has made advances to the Imperial Munitions Board at Ottawa of $116,000,000 to date, and we have agreed to advance them a further sum of $34,000,000, for which I have the money provided. That makes a total of $150,000,000 which the Government of Canada will have advanced to the Imperial Government for the purpose of buying munitions and supplies in Canada. We owe the Imperial Government in London about $97,000,000. So there is at present a balance owing us by the Imperial Government of about $18,000,000.

Is that $97,000,000 over
and above the $122,000,000 just mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. With regard to that $97,000,000, we could either issue out securities, which they could pledge in New York in connection with further loans there,

or we could set it off against this larger sum which they will owe us.
My hon. friend has asked me about the banks. The Dominion Government, as I have stated, has loaned or arranged to loan $150,000,000. We made arrangements with the banks to loan $100,000,000 direct to the Imperial Government. The Dominion Government is not guarantor of those loans, as it was not regarded as necessary that the Imperial credit should be fortified by the Dominion credit.

I did not mean
that the guarantee was necessary, but that the hanks might have desired it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. The first
$75,000,000 loan was against the security of British treasury hills, and then there was a further loan of $24,000,000, making a total of $100,000,000. The last $50,000,000 which the Dominion Government advanced to the Imperial Government was borrowed by us from the banks. In that case it was loaned direct to us.
That Iasi, $50,000,000 borrowed from the banks was in connection with the $100,000,000 war loan recently issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. We borrowed the amount from the banks and loaned it to the Imperial Government.
Can the minister give us any idea of what the debt of the country will be at the end of the present fiscal year? I should like to know what we shall owe in Canada, and what in London.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thought some
hon. gentlemen might desire that information, and I have had a memorandum prepared.

To what date
does this memorandum go?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From 1914 to the end of last month. This memorandum shows in round figures that the net national debt to March 31, 1914, was $335,000,000-that is, up to The end of the last fiscal period bef ore the war broke out. The amount of the national debt to March 31, 1915, was $449,000,000; to March 31, 1915, $615,000,000; and to January 31, 1917, $745,000,000.

Does that include our
liabilities .to the British Government for munitions and other war supplies? I do not want to press this question if for any reason the minister might think it inadvisable to answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What I have
given is a correct statement of the national debt to January 31, 1917, namely, $745,000,000; that represents the debt so far as ascertained. My hon. friend is aware that Great Britain supplies our troops on the continent with such equipment as they may require at the front, such, as .rations, munitions, and other supplies.
Has this liability been liquidated up to date?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The liability has not been ascertained up to date. Since the last session of Parliament an arrangement has been come to, whereby the British Government will be paid six shillings per day per man for rations, clothing and equipment of every kind whatsoever, munitions, small arms, artillery, etc., supplied to the Canadian forces at the front. In our view, that charge is quite fair and reasonable.
That includes rations and clothing? -

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Everything.
When was the last settlement made on that basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The adjustment has not yet been made. I am speaking from memory. But I can get the information for my hon. friend, if desired.
Would there be any substantial amount due on that account?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It might be a matter of $50,000,000 or $60,000,000. At all events the arrangement is so fair that the amount in terms of waT finance is not large.

It looks very
reasonable.
Am I to conclude frpm the statement the minister has just given, that the total debt of Canada up to January 31 will be, roughly speaking, $800,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is a fairly accurate estimate.

I understood the minister to say that the $745,000,000 does not include the open , accounts between the two 'Governments; that is, the British Government owe us $150,000,000, we will say, and we pwe them $97,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the net debt. I think about $800,000,000 represents the situation.
That includes the $50,000,000 the minister just spoke of as being due under the new system of adjustment? But the net debt does not include the adjustment of the open accounts5

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot say
definitely as to that, but my opinion is this. They owe us more than we owe them on open account, and I think-I am not positive-that the principle of set-off has been applied, and that $745,000,000 represents the net debt.
That is, you have charged them with your open -account and credited them with their open account?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

In view of our large revenue, I was rather surprised -to hear the -minister -say that this proposed loan was for ordinary account. Does he not anticipate that the revenue will be large enough -to pay the expenditures on current account? I should -also like to know why the minister thinks that the last war loan would not have been subscribed on a -straight five per cent basis, after paying one-quarter per cent commission to the brokers. The loan was issued at 97j. I have often wondered if it would not have been subscribed and more than subscribed on a -straight five per cent and at par.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Yes, I understood that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A year ago last fall the Imperial Government put out in the United States a five per cent five-year loan at 98, the underwriters taking a considerable portion of it at 96. That loan went down to 95, to 94, to 93. When Canada comes on the market with her securities, she is to a certain extent in competition with those Imperial securities and in competition with that market price. Canada's credit today is better on this continent than Great Britain's credit. We can sell our securities on a lower interest basis than Great Britain can sell her securities in the United States. Of course, Great Britain has offered no securities in Canada. Answering my hon. friend's question specifically:. At the time that we made the loan last fall of $100,000,000, our fifteen year securities, payable in New York, were slightly under par; that is to say, that was the quotation for a- market lot.
About 99J.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The five per cent fifteen-year securities which we had issued the previous March were about 991. Now, if I had attempted to sell $100,000,000 to the public at par, of course, I could not have done it. You have to put your securities out at a lower rate than the stock exchange quotation, because you are selling wholesale, and it is of supreme importance that your loan should go to a premium. If your loan goes to a discount, you are not so welcome the next time you come along. There is such a thing as a prudent generosity in connection with loans, especially to your own people, and it is much better to put out a loan at 971 and have it run up a point or a point and a half by reason of over-subscription, than to have it go to a discount a point or a point and a half, because that injures your credit. We have been very successful in regard to our loans, every loan put out in the United States by the Dominion of Canada having gone to a substantial premium. The last loan put out stands just about the issue price, but it did run up to 99 or a little over. The best proof of our financing is the market quotations for our loans after they were issued and subsequently our credit has been im-

proved by our loans, because every time we have made a loan, it has been open to any subscriber to take a small profit if he has so desired. That has been by reason of the heavy over-subscription and the popular demand for the loans.

I thoroughly understood what the hon minister told us befoi'e, that it is necessary to issue a loan at a price a little lower than the market price. I quite appreciate that in connection with loans issued in the United States or Great Britain. This, however, was a loan to the people, and we are not told how much of that loan was taken up by the people and how much by the loan companies and the banks. The loan companies and the banks, of course, would want to get the security at a price at which they could resell it at a profit; but the ordinary man or woman who bought $1,000 or $2,000, was, so far as my knowledge goes, perfectly satisfied with the five per cent Government loan as he was getting only three per cent from the banks. But the price at which the loan could be sold afterwards would depend entirely on how much of the $100,000,000 was taken up by the loan companies and the banks and how much was taken up by the private investors. That was why I asked the question; it was not because I did not know that it was necessary for the minister to issue loans in the way described by him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the case of a loan as large as $100,000,000, you have to rely on all classes of the community to contribute. The small investors could not subscribe nearly as much as the larger investors. It would take ten thousand $1,000 subscriptions to make $10,000,000. You get subscriptions from the small investor; you get subscriptions from the business man who can subscribe for $25,000 or $30,000; you get them from capitalists who will take $100,000 or $200,000 or even more; you get them from the life insurance companies who will subscribe for large amounts, according to the state of their finances, and you get subscriptions from other companies. The banks took none of the last issue, because my arrangement with them was that the public was to have the first call. My hon. friend has it in mind that if the public would take the loan on a five per cent basis, it should be put out on that basis. That is not quite sound, for this reason, that notwithstanding you are putting out a loan for patriotic purposes, such as the prosecution bf the war, it is always wise to observe the financial or business conditions. The patriotic aspect of it creates a certain atmosphere which is favourable, but your loan must conform with market conditions or, even if immediately successful, it will go to a discount later on. In other words, it must conform with the prevailing financial conditions applicable to that class of security; otherwise, investors will subscribe for it under patriotic impulse, hold it for a little while, and then sell it out and buy something more attractive. I am quite clear that your loan must be such as, in the estimation of the investing public, m.akes it a desirable investment at the time when it is put out.
In regard to the three per cent certificates which have been issued, what rate do they pay and are they transferable to future loans?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The three-year
war saving certificates are sold at the rate of $86 for $100 denominations,. $43 for $50 denominations, and $21.50 for $25 denominations. The rate of interest is slightly over 5 per cent.
They do not bear interest, but are payable at par?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

Are they in
debenture form?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They are really
like debenture stock. They are made out in the name of the party who buys them. He may surrender or transfer them according to the terms of the issue, but he cannot by losing his certificate be deprived of his property in it. One reason why we made them payable to the party purchasing is because most people of slender means have no safety-deposit boxes in wihich to place their securities.

Did I correctly understand
the minister to say that in 1914, the national debt was $335,000,000 and that at the close of the present fiscal year it would be about $800,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On January 31,
1917.
What proportion of that increase is due to the war expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot answer
that off-hand, but it will be gratifying to my hon. friend to know that during the present fiscal year our revenues have been such as will enable us to pay all our ordin-

ary and all onr capital expenditure, and, I think, pTOibaby 560,000,000 or $70,000,000 on account of the principal of our war expenditure. The first year after the war broke out there was a deficit on account of capital and ordinary account amounting to some $40,000,000 or $50,000,000. That was because out revenues were at once affected by the dislocation of business occasioned by the outbreak of war. Since that time our revenues have been such as to enable us to carry on our ordinary and capital expenditure and to pay a considerable amount on account of the principal of our war indebtedness.
What was the cost of the flotation of the last loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should say
about three-quarters of one per cent, or less.
What would be the total amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
I noticed in the
Financial Times a discussion of what was said to be a warning by the minister to the investing public of Canada against investing in English securities. A quotation was made from the Toronto News, which spoke in the very strongest terms of the moral obliquity of the man who would venture to do that. The Financial Times rather questioned the right of the Finance Minister to take such a strong stand. Is it a fact that the Finance Minister has intimated, either directly or indirectly, that he does not think it wise for Canadians to take up any of the English loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no hesitation in saying that the Canadian investing public should reserve their funds for Dominion loans. In Great Britain no issues are allowed outside of Government issues except with the consent of the Treasury. Great Britain borrows money in the United States, where there is a plethora of money.

Bolling in gold, they
say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Great Britain
uses that money to make purchases in the United States. If the Canadian public buy British securities issued in New York, Canadian money is being used for the purpose of making purchases in the United States. That in itself would not he objectionable if it were not for its possible effect upon our exchanges. International balances, as my hon. friend knows, are settled in gold and

if the Canadian public invested largely in British or French loans made in New York for the purpose of buying goods in the United States, exchange would soon become unfavourable to Canada. Apart from that, when the Dominion Government would make its next war loan in Canada the money which would otherwise have been available to take up those issues would have been spent in the United States. What I have said is subject to this qualification: A considerable portion of the loans which we float in Canada find their way to the United States. If we put out a loan of $100,000,000 in Canada, $15,000,000, $20,000,000, or $25,000,000 of it may be sold in the United States by those who took it. That, of course, would he a set-off against $15,000,000, $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 that might he expended by Canadian people in purchasing securities in New York. As long as exchange is not seriously affected and as long as the loan fund in Canada is not depleted so that our loans are unlikely to he subscribed, no harm will be done. But on account of the large sums that we require for our own war expenditures and to finance Great Britain in her purchase of munitions in Canada, it is exceedingly desirable that the Canadian people should conserve their resources for the purpose of buying our war loans. That is not discriminating against Great Britain. The authorities in Great Britain would he the first to suggest that the Canadian people should not purchase those loans in the United States, because there is abundance of money there to take up those loans, and Great Britain is not in any way disadvantaged. I do not hesitate to say that I view those purchases as inadvisable. Answer might be made to me: If a Canadian buys a security in the American market and is able to sell it later at a profit, is that not a gain? It is a gain to the individual, and, in a sense, to the nation. But there is an overriding consideration, and that is that the money has been diverted from the issues which the Dominion Government may offer to the Canadian public. Although the individual may make a profit, the national power to finance itself is weakened.

The minister has talked all around the point. I merely wanted to know whether or not the hon. gentleman intimated to the investing public in Canada that they should not invest in the British War Loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not recollect precisely what I said, but I did give an

intimation that I thought it exceedingly desirable that the Canadian investing public should conserve their funds for Dominion war loans and should not buy loans of any government issued in New York, because there is abundance of money in New York to take up those securities. In that I am in entire accord with the Imperial Government. No possible question arises as to' the Imperial Treasury. They do not ask the Canadian people to buy loans which they are issuing in New York for the purpose of purchasing munitions in America, because they know perfectly well that we require to make our own war loans here and to supply money to pay for the munitions which they order here. If a situation arose in which the people of Canada were buying seourities so extensively in the United States as to seriously affect the exchanges, or seriously affect our prospects of floating our loans in Canada, I should have no hesitation in saying that the Dominion Government should put a tax upon any securities so purchased. I must decline to commit myself as to whether we shall take that course or not; it depends on events.

The minister said that our buoyant revenues would fully meet our ordinary expenditure and pay for the interest on some $40,000,000 of war loans. Can the minister inform us now what part of the revenue is formed by the war taxes imposed? That is, the business profits war tax and the stamps and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot give it accurately. For this the first year the result of the business profits war tax will, I think, exceed $10,000,000. Next year the amount will be much larger, because profits for the past year have been very much greater than they were for 1915. The special tax upon the banks realizes about $1,000,000. As to what the stamp and other taxes realize, I am not prepared to say, because I did not know that this question would arise. Those matters are usually dealt with in the Budget.
Does the minister intend to exercise any control over stock exchange operations in order to control our financial strength for domestic loans?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All these questions have had a good deal of thought on my part. I need not say that they are very difficult questions to deal with. We have a boundary line of 3,600 miles between us and the United States. There are numerous financial transactions across that line every day. In my own opinion, the best way to deal with the situation- is to watch the exchanges. If our Canadian exchange is maintained, then their purchases over here of our securities and commodities are equalling our purchases over there. If the exchange began to run against us, we might have to take drastic measures with regard to the purchase of securities on the other side. But the exchange at present is quite satisfactory. -

Has the minister ever taken into consideration the question of the succession duty taxation imposed by the provinces? So far as Ontario is concerned, loans to the Ontario Government or securities sold by the Ontario Government are exempt from succession duty tax. If the provinces could see their way clear to applying the same thing to Dominion domestic loans, I think it would help the flotation of the war loans materially. A great many people buy provincial loans, having that object in view, knowing that whatever they have invested in these securities will not be liable to the succession duties which are fairly large. I know it would probably interfere to a considerable extent with the revenues of the provinces, but this is a time when we are all bending every energy to meet the war conditions, and the expenditure in connection with the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When our first loan was being floated I took up the question privately with the prime ministers of the several provinces, and they were not unanimous as to the advisability of this course. This was not through any lack of desire on their part to be patriotic and to do everything they could to facilitate the prosecution of the war; their objection was rather on this ground, that a province which has to depend for its revenues upon taxation should not make securities free of taxation to a greater extent than is absolutely necessary, because people will take advantage of such a condition and purchase those securities for the express purpose of evading the tax. If you had enough securities of one kind free of succession duty to absorb a considerable demand the province would be deprived of a large amount of its taxes. In England they are careful not to create a large class of securities that would be free of income tax.

I think there is a great deal in what the Finance Minister has said.

I would be very sorry, indeed, to see this Government embark on any scheme which would in any way relieve any portion of the community from its due share of taxation. I think the time has come in Canada when every person and every class of, person should be taught that they must pay their share of taxation. I know that along the lines mentioned by the Minister of Finance a number of fairly large loans were issued by the province of New Brunswick in the last year and a half which were made tax-exempt in New Brunswick. The result was that there was an unprecedented rush for those bonds, and while they were on the market I think very few of the war bonds were absorbed. Those provincial bonds were all taken up six or eight months ago, and when the last loan was issued there was a very much more hearty response through the province of New Brunswick than in the previous case. I would suggest to the Finance Minister that he might take some steps to prevent, if possible, the floating of any other loans in Canada excepting war loans. I realize the difficulties.

What could
he do?

I realize that there are difficulties; I simply want to know whether he could not go into the matter and see if something could not be done. It might be done by a super-tax, or a tax of some kind. From the statement given to us to-day, it seems to me that before this war is over we are going to require all the money we can possibly raise in Canada to enable us to do our share.

The minister told us to-day that the public debt of Canada is $745,000,000 at this moment, and that at the end of the fiscal year it will be $800,000,000; and then we will start with this loan of $100,000,000 which we are authorizing. Is it premature to ask my hon. friend how much more he will have to borrow during the next fiscal year, $1917-18? Perhaps he cannot give us the answer to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think I can
tell my hon. friend approximately. We may need from $200,000,000 to $250,000,000 for our own war expenditures on this side, and we should borrow considerable sums in addition to that for the purpose of establishing the credits here out of which Great Britain can pay for the munitions which she ie ordering here.

To come back to the question of investment, if I understood the minister, the Government control the issues of new debentures or stocks that are issued to the public. It occurred to me that it might be a good thing for the Government to at least control some of the mining issues that have been offered and are still being offered to the Canadian public. I have never known a time when more literature came to a man's office, offering attractive prices for mines in a neighbouring province. We know that periodically there runs across this continent a mining boom, and there seems to be one on now. I think it is time for the Government to step in and stop these operators, who, I believe, are 5 p.m. largely people .in the United States, gathering up Canadian money .and selling what is really a hole in the ground. I think it would be well for the minister to look into that -and, if possible, control that sort of investment in our country. There is another feature in connection with this, though perhaps .it does not affect the Department of the Minister of Finance. These people are loading down the Canadian .mails with circular letters that are carried for one cent a letter, whereas the people of Canada are paying three cents a letter to do legitimate business. I think it is time for the Government to step in and control this sort of work.

Can the minister state
the rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not advisable to state it, and there is no loan immediately in prospect. As things -are, unless conditions radically change, it would be a five per -cent security; but of course I cannot state -at what price it would be issued. The price is never fixed until the time of issue. That is a matter for consideration, -and, if it is sold in the United States, a matter for negotiation.

The reason I ask that in conversation not long since with -a party who was speaking of making some investment, it was pointed out to me that the short-term British loan, I think, is paying about six per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nobody knows it better than I do.
It puts the minister in a difficult position in competition with the British loan if it is issued at six per cent and we issue at only five per cent.
Can the minister tell us *v\ hat the oust of the war has been up to date; and whether we have reached the maximum of expenditure for the coming year?
I may say that the loan to which I referred is a short-term loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I explained when my hon. friend was out, that we are always in competition with the securities that are issued in the United States; but our credit is really higher on this continent than the credit of Great Britain, and consequently we are able to sell our securities on a lower interest basis than she is.
The minister has never been asked for collateral.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have never been asked for collateral, and I do not think that we shall be. Nevertheless, my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) is right. We are affected in our issues by the price at which Great Britain issues her securities.
My hon. friend (Mr. Maroil) has asked about the war expenditure. The war expenditure to January 31, 1917, in Canada and Great Britain is about $450,000,000. Then there is the adjusted situation on the Continent; I cannot say how much that will be at the present time.
Can the minister give us the probable expenditure for another twelve months?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should not like to make an estimate.
Are there any securities falling, due this year on which this loan will be dependent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are two short-date loans, aggregating $50,000,000, due in April and May. We have a $25,000,000 loan maturing in New York on August 1, and then we are clear, I think, until past the end of the year. I may say that in our financing we are keeping free of short-date obligations as much as possible.

In inviting subscriptions for these loans, has the minister considered the advisability of using the post offices? There are many places where there are no branch banks, and if these notes were offered in small denominations at the var- ' ious post offices throughout the country some money might be raised. It might be
in small sums, but still it would be of value at a time like this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are on sale at post office savings branches.

I have not
seen the report of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but I would ask whether these loan subscriptions have come from the post office savings banks, or whether they have come out of the current business of the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They have come from both sources. I do not think the post office saving deposits have been seriously affected.
